L17: # The Cape Churchill Herd
L18: 
L19: ## Wapusk National Park
L20: ## What makes a caribou, a caribou?
L21: 
L22:   * Their Latin name (Scientific name): Rangifer tarandus.
L23:   * Member of the deer family (Cervidae) along with moose, deer and elk.
L24:   * The word “caribou” comes from Mi'kmaq “xalibu”, meaning “who digs for food”.
L25:   * Unlike others within the deer family, both male and female caribou have antlers.
L26: #### The Eastern Migratory Caribou
L27: 
L28:   * The two main herds that use the Wapusk region are the Qamanirjuaq Herd (Barren-ground caribou) and the Cape Churchill herd (Eastern Migratory caribou).
L29:   * This EduKit focuses on the Eastern Migratory, Cape Churchill Caribou herd.
L30: 
L31: 
L32: 
L33: cite5†Image: An illustration of Parks Canada mascot Parka with a thoughtful expression and a lightbulb next to her head.†pcweb2.azureedge.net L34: 
L35: Parka Fact
L36: Just like snowflakes, no two antlers are ever the same!
L37: ## Facts about the Cape Churchill Caribou
L38: 
L39:   * Population counts suggest the size of the Cape Churchill herd has varied from 1,000 to 3,000 caribou over the past 25 years.
L40:   * The Cape Churchill herd is a unique forest-tundra ecotype, which describes the area they live in. A large portion of their habitat is protected within Wapusk National Park.
L41: ## What do they eat?
L42: 
L43:   * Their main food source is lichen. Lichen is a mix of algae and fungi that fuse together.
L44:   * To stay healthy, caribou eat over 2 garbage bags full of lichen every day!
L45:   * They also have been known to eat willow and birch branches, berries, grasses, sedges and even mushrooms at times.

L57: What is your favourite meal? Could you eat 2 garbage bags full of it each day?
L58: cite6†Image: An illustration of Parks Canada mascot Parka with her hand on her chin and a thought bubble containing a question mark next to her head.†pcweb2.azureedge.net L59: #### How long do caribou live?
L60: 
L61: Caribou live for about 15 years!
L62: 
L63: #### Are reindeer and caribou the same animal?
L64: 
L65: Yes! They belong to the same genus and species.
L66: 
L67: In North America, we use the name “caribou”, while in Europe and Asia they typically use the name “reindeer”.
L68: #### Do caribou make noise?
L69: 
L70:   * They make many sounds! Including grunting and bellowing.
L71:   * You may also hear a clicking sound when caribou are on the move. That sound comes from a tendon rolling around a small bone in their foot. Some think the clicking helps individuals stay close together in a snowstorm or when it’s super foggy.

L79: Bulls are male caribou, cows are female caribou, and calves are baby caribou.

L87: Caribou are very important to many Indigenous peoples. What do caribou mean to you?

L91: cite7†Image: A caribou stands on grass in the background while facing a trail camera in the foreground.†pcweb2.azureedge.net Curious bull looking at a trail camera.
L92: #### Do antlers stay on forever?
L93: 
L94:   * Antlers grow and shed every year.
L95:   * For males (bulls), antlers are shed after the fall rut in October/November (they no longer need them to impress). Their antlers can weigh up to 25 pounds. That’s about 3 milk jugs!
L96:   * For females (cows), antlers are not shed until after they’ve given birth as they use their antlers to defend their food. Their antlers can weigh up to 8 pounds!
L97: #### What are antlers made of?
L98: 
L99:   * Bone! They are protected and wrapped with velvet skin which helps them grow.
L100: 
L101: cite8†Image: Four caribou standing on grass. A body of water is in the foreground.†pcweb2.azureedge.net Cows looking for food.
L102: #### Are caribou dangerous to people?
L103: 
L104:   * Caribou are known to be very docile animals and would prefer to be left alone. Always remember, these are wild animals and to be respectful and cautious.
L105: 
L106: Have you HERD?
L107: 
L108:   * Wapusk National Park is home to approximately 300 species of lichen!
L109:   * They are found in forested areas, as well as on the tundra, on rocks, trees and human-made structures within the park!
